title: Fix the abbreviation lookup and stop an enumerator dot ending a sentence
action:
FIX-FIRST, and READ THE BOUND AT THE END BEFORE YOU START. An independent judge broke the citation boundary rule for the second time. It did not read the tests — it copied `normalize`, `is_terminator`, `NON_TERMINAL_ABBREVIATIONS`, `is_sentence_end`, `quote_resolves` and `citation_quote` byte-for-byte out of the module, compiled them, and probed. Two defects, both real bugs rather than heuristic gaps:

DEFECT 1 — the abbreviation lookup is defeated by ONE adjacent character. `is_sentence_end` (mod.rs:709-725) matches the set by byte equality on the space-delimited token, so a leading bracket or quote slips straight past it:
  proposal: "We should not follow lane-b (i.e. cache the token on the worker side."
  citation: "cache the token on the worker side"  -> PASSES today, and inverts the lane.
The judge confirmed all 28 combinations of a leading `(`, `\"`, `'`, `[`, `-`, `*`, em dash and `:` against i.e./e.g./etc./cf. `(i.e. ...)` is the single most common written form of the abbreviation this rule was added for.

DEFECT 2 — an ENUMERATOR dot ends a sentence. `1.` is not in the set, so:
  proposal: "We must not do any of the following:\n\n1. Cache the token on the worker side.\n2. Skip the lease check."
  citation: "cache the token on the worker side"  -> PASSES today.
Same for `a.` and `ii.`. A markdown numbered list under a negated stem is ordinary design prose, not an exotic input. The END side mirrors it: "Cache the token on the worker side 1. only when the lease is dead and gone." cited as "Cache the token on the worker side 1." passes.

DEFECT 3 — the comment block OVER-CLAIMS, and that is a defect of the same weight as the other two. mod.rs:682-684 states as fact that requiring the span to sit between two sentence boundaries 'makes that strip impossible WITHIN a sentence'. The two probes above are within-sentence strips that succeed, so the headline claim is false and contradicts the block's own bullet at :700.

WHAT TO DO.
1. Probes FIRST, one per defect, run red before you touch the rule: the `(i.e.` form, the numbered-list form, and the end-side enumerator mirror. Cover at least `(` and `\"` for defect 1 and at least `1.` and `a.` for defect 2.
2. Fix defect 1 by trimming leading non-alphanumeric bytes from the token BEFORE the set lookup. Do not widen the set to spell out punctuated variants — that is the same bug with more rows.
3. Fix defect 2 by treating a token as non-terminal when, with its trailing dot removed, it is entirely digits, or one to three ASCII letters that are all lowercase or all uppercase (covering `a.`, `ii.`, `iv.`). Comment why that shape is an enumerator and not a word.
4. Fix defect 3 by rewriting mod.rs:682-684. The true claim is that the whole-sentence rule RAISES THE COST of a negation strip and refuses the written forms the rule enumerates; it does NOT make one impossible. Say that, and keep the existing bullets that already name the framing miss.
5. Every existing `verbs::blind` test stays green and none is edited. If one goes red, that is information about your fix.

PROHIBITIONS. Do not weaken MIN_CITATION_CHARS, MIN_CITATION_WORDS, the per-lane scoping, or any other check. Do not delete or relax the framing probe at mod.rs:1776-1783 — that limit is decided by decision 79b5437b and stays pinned green.

THE BOUND, and it is part of the cell. This is the LAST rung on the boundary rule. If a judge breaks it again, the answer is NOT a fourth fix: it is to stop claiming the check resists negation stripping at all and to reduce the claim to bare whole-sentence provenance. So when you write the comment in step 4, write it as though this were already the final state — no promise that another case will be handled later, no wording that invites rung four.

Right call, loudly recorded, not a quiet narrowing. normalize (mod.rs:658) lowercases every ASCII char before the scan, so the cell's 'all uppercase' half is dead code. The literal 'one to three lowercase letters' shape would make 'one.' an enumerator, so the control proposal ending 'a live one.' (mod.rs:1293) would stop resolving; well_formed() with that citation backs 26 call sites, so double-digit reds are the expected blast radius and 14 is plausible. The narrow shape's own cost (ab., A1., xl. still read as sentence ends) is named in the comment at :715-717 and in the trace

Mechanically confirmed rather than taken on trust: the 6eaf4955 versions of the same functions, compiled standalone, return PASS for all five probe forms, so all five probes were necessarily RED pre-fix. None can pass vacuously - each pins the exact reason string, so an over-refusal for a different reason also fails

36 probes run. Everything that passes falls inside a limit the comment already names: unlisted abbreviations (Dr., U.S., a.m.), markers outside the shape (ab., A1., xl.), and the decided framing case. REFUTED attacks: decimals, spaced version numbers, dotted filenames, CJK and unicode terminators, quoted and parenthesised sentences, dot-before-newline, single initials, end-side ellipsis. No input found where a citation clears the floors, resolves, and inverts meaning outside the enumerated limits

mod.rs:796 'hay[from..].find(needle)' with from = start + 1 (mod.rs:810) slices MID-CHARACTER when the needle's first char is multibyte and an occurrence fails the boundary check. Reproduced through the exact pipeline: proposal 'He said “cache the token on the worker side” loudly today.' with citation '“cache the token on the worker side' clears both floors (35 chars, 7 words) then PANICS: 'byte index 9 is not a char boundary; it is inside curly-quote (bytes 8..11 of string)'. Same with a leading em dash. normalize (:647-661) preserves non-ASCII, so the :787-788 assumption that the scan is over ASCII bytes is false, and bee blind check aborts with a Rust panic instead of the typed refusal - reachable by any dossier whose citation starts with a smart quote or dash copied from rendered prose

The truth holds as currently worded: every written form the boundary rule enumerates - plain '.', ', i.e.', '...', '(i.e.', '"e.g.', '1.', 'a.', 'ii.' on the start side and the enumerator on the end side - is refused, and the rule's own comment states it RAISES THE COST rather than making a strip impossible. No surviving over-claim beyond provenance anywhere in refusal text or comments
